guards.rule: null
Every parametric stair with an open side must automatically include a safety railing or guard on that open side.
Every stair opening in a corridor or hall must automatically include a safety railing or guard on its open edges.
A wardrobe model must read as a storage unit (doors, handles, depth); a flat wall-panel model with an embedded window frame is a wrong model for the type and must be swapped.
Scene check S5 failures (detached elements) are resolved by re-running the build stage so the join/attach pass re-evaluates the scene.
A ceiling light with no hang record (cord/rod/canopy) is a build-stage omission; re-running build regenerates the hang geometry.
A sofa whose parts stand more than 1 cm apart is a build-stage join failure; re-running build re-runs soft_seats.join_parts. A swap to an audited-removed asset is refused.
Scene check S1 geometry failures are resolved by re-running the build stage.
Scene check S2 geometry failures are resolved by re-running the build stage.

When rotate_piece is refused because every candidate orientation lowers the plausibility score (the piece cannot face its group without breaking F4/F6), the furniture agent's next round must re-place the piece, not just rotate it.
A piece reaching through the room outline by less than 0.03 m (3 cm) is within tolerance and is not a real finding.

A parametric piece whose drawn footprint is larger than every library model in its type (e.g. a 0.80 m drawn coffee table vs 0.78 m max models) must be built at its drawn size, not shrunk to a library model, so it does not collide with its neighbours; the collision is then resolved by moving the neighbour, not the drawn anchor.

An armchair that is drawn behind the back of a sofa (looking at it) and whose every rotation either leaves it facing the sofa's back or faces a wall within 0.12 m must be re-placed by the group solver, not rotated in place; the seating group's orientation is solved as a unit around the sofa.

An armchair that is drawn at a distance and angle from its seating group that no single rotation or small move can bring within the group's facing and distance limits must be re-placed by the group solver, not rotated in place; the seating group's orientation is solved as a unit around the sofa.
A dining chair needs ≥ 0.81 m from the table edge to the wall or piece behind it; the solver must place chairs with that clearance and the inspector must flag any chair short of it.
A sofa's back must rest on a wall (or a fixed piece); the solver must not leave a sofa floating in the middle of a room, and the inspector must flag any sofa whose back is off a wall.

An armchair in a seating group must face the group (the sofa/coffee table it belongs to); the solver must orient armchairs toward their group and the inspector must flag any armchair that does not face it.
A double bed needs ≥ 0.60 m of free walkway along each side; the solver must place the bed with that clearance and the inspector must flag any bed short of it.
A nightstand must not stand in front of a window (it blocks the opening and the light); the solver must place nightstands clear of windows and the inspector must flag any that block one.
A wardrobe needs ≥ 0.80 m of free space in front to open its doors; the solver must place wardrobes with that clearance and the inspector must flag any short of it.

A shower must be a real product size (a standard shower tray/cabine); the solver must not build a shower at a size no product has, and the inspector must flag any shower outside the type's product sizes.

A bed must keep at least 0.60 m of free clearance on its open side; when the drawn position cannot provide it, the solver must re-place the bed (or swap to a narrower model) rather than accept the tight fit.
A wardrobe must have at least 0.80 m of free space in front for its doors to open; the solver must re-place it or choose a shallower model when the drawn position blocks this clearance.
The free zone in front of a sofa must not be blocked by another piece; the solver must arrange the seating group so the sofa's front is clear.
A coffee table must be positioned in front of the sofa it serves; the solver must place it within the seating group's front zone.
An armchair in a seating group must be within 2.50 m of the coffee table and oriented within 30° of it; the solver must place it accordingly.
A dining chair must have at least 0.81 m of clearance behind it (from table edge to wall or piece); the solver must ensure this in the dining group layout.
A dining table must not stand in front of a window, blocking the view and light; the solver must place the dining group away from windows.
A dining chair must not stand in front of a window, blocking the view and light; the solver must place the dining group away from windows.
A wall cabinet in a kitchen must use a realistic model with proper materials and detail, not a crude low-poly placeholder.

Site areas labeled in the documents (pools, sunning platforms, parking) must be built with outlines and appropriate models; the site stage must read and construct all labeled site areas, not just the building.
When two levels are at the same elevation and contain near-identical duplicate rooms, the reading stage must detect this as a duplicated floor and merge them, not build both.
A potted plant placed by the decor stage must be preserved through the agent stage; if it is removed, the agent must re-add it or record the reason.

The agent stage must not drop a placed decor piece (a potted_plant) that the decor stage built and that the room's program allows; a piece is removed only when a code check refuses it, and the removal must be recorded.

The agent stage must not drop a placed piece (an armchair) that the decor stage built and that the room's program allows; a piece is removed only when a code check refuses it, and the removal must be recorded.

The agent stage must not drop a placed piece (a side_table) that the decor stage built and that the room's program allows; a piece is removed only when a code check refuses it, and the removal must be recorded.

A stove drawn as part of a kitchen run must be built as a member of that run (the run's model carries the hob); the build stage must not leave a planned stove without a scene object when its kitchen run is present.
A sink drawn as part of a kitchen run must be built as a member of that run; the build stage must not leave a planned sink without a scene object when its kitchen run is present.

When two floor_lamp footprints of the same room overlap by more than 30%, the smaller is a duplicate drawing of the larger (a lamp drawn twice), not a second lamp; the larger is kept and the smaller is not built, and this is a correct drop, not a loss.

When two floor_lamp footprints of the same room overlap by more than 15%, the smaller is a duplicate drawing of the larger (a lamp drawn twice), not a second lamp; the larger is kept and the smaller is not built, and this is a correct drop, not a loss.
A small footprint (an ottoman) drawn more than 80% inside an armchair's footprint is the armchair's seat cushion, not a separate piece; it is not built, and this is a correct drop, not a loss.
none

A section or elevation layer (a layer whose name carries a view marker such as 'görünüş' or that holds only the stair's profile) is not plan geometry: the model builds the stair from the plan layer and the section layer is recorded as a view, not as a lost element.
A layer whose name carries a view marker such as 'görünüş' (elevation) is a view, not plan geometry: it is recorded as a view and not flagged as a lost element.

A layer that holds only decorative detail geometry (arcs, curves, thin lines) and no INSERT blocks is a detail/decoration layer, not a furniture layer: it is recorded as decoration and not flagged as a lost element.

A decor element whose host piece is not built must not be silently dropped: the build stage must either build the host or record each dependent decor element as lost with the host's id, so the loss is visible and reviewable.

Furniture symbols on a furniture layer (e.g. 'A-TEFRIS') are buildable content, not unbuildable annotations: the build stage must type and build them, or record each as lost with a reason, never skip the whole layer.

Site areas labelled in the plan (parking, terrace, pool) are buildable site content: the build stage must build their outlines from site.paving/parking/grass, or record each as lost with a reason, never skip them as 'exterior labels'.
A stove drawn with its back parallel to a wall and a small gap behind it belongs on the wall: the reading stage must snap its back to the wall, not leave a visible gap.
A kitchen room's program requires a fridge: when the kitchen run is built without one, the build stage must complete the run with the missing fridge, not leave the room without it.
A toilet needs at least 0.38 m from the side wall or fixture on each side: the reading stage must place it with that clearance, not 0.33 m.
A bathtub needs at least 0.53 m clear in front: the reading stage must place it with that clearance, not 0.28 m.
A shower needs at least 0.53 m clear in front: the reading stage must place it with that clearance, not 0.27 m.

A shower or bathtub in a bathroom smaller than about 6 m2 must be placed so its front clearance is at least 0.53 m; when the drawn bay cannot give that clearance, the fixture is swapped for a walk-in shower or a shorter tub that fits the bay, never left with a sub-code front gap.

A toilet must have at least 0.38 m from its centre to the nearest side wall or fixture; when the drawn position cannot give that, the toilet is moved along its wall or the neighbouring fixture is shifted, not left 0.33 m from the wall.
A bathtub must have at least 0.53 m clear in front; when the room cannot give that, the tub is swapped for a shorter model or repositioned, never left with 0.28 m.
A bedroom render must frame the bed as the anchor; the camera is posed to show the bed in full, not cut out of the frame.
A room whose documents label it a living or activity room and whose area exceeds 30 m2 is typed living, not other, so its full program (tv, seating, dining) is built.
A bathroom set is complete only when it carries every fixture the documents draw in that bathroom; a missing tall_cabinet is added by completing the set, not left out.
A hall on a floor above the entrance has no shoe-off program and no storage program; it is furnished only with a stair and, if drawn, a console or coat hook, never a shoe_cabinet or wardrobe.
A terrace or balcony larger than 10 m2 is furnished with a full outdoor seating and dining set (multiple chairs, a table, planters) matching the documents, not a single chair and plant.
Site areas labelled in the documents (pool, sunning terrace, parking) are built as outlines in the model; a labelled site area with no outline is a loss, not an omission.

A living room with a tv_unit must also carry a media wall or feature wall behind the TV, a rug under the seating group, and at least one floor lamp or pendant; a bare wall behind the TV is a missing set, not a finished room.
An opening whose ray hits its own wall is not cut through it: the build must cut the opening through the wall it is assigned to, not leave the wall solid.
A stair flight with an open side must be built with a continuous balustrade and handrail over its full run, with newels at turns and ends; a wall handrail where a flight has no open side.

A wall-hung item (mirror, art, shelf) must not be placed on a wall span that is covered by a standing piece (wardrobe, cabinet) whose top reaches over the item's bottom; the decor stage must move it to a free wall span or leave it out.
A wall-hung item must not be placed over a window or door opening on its wall; the decor stage must move it to a solid wall span or leave it out.
The camera set must include a frontal view of the entrance facade, square to it, showing the main door.
When the terrain slopes steeper than 1:3 against the building, a retaining edge (wall or stepped plinth) must be built along the affected facade.
A kitchen counter's top must be at its working height (0.90-0.97 m); the build stage must use a model or parametric height that matches, not a model whose top is above working height.
A bathroom interior view must show the washbasin and its mirror in frame, not just a tub rim; the camera must be posed to include the basin and mirror.

A bathroom interior view showing a bathtub must include its taps/mixer and at least one surrounding design element (mirror, shelf, or adjacent fixture) so it reads as a designed feature, not a bare object.

A bathroom washbasin is never placed without a mirror above it and a styled wall finish (accent panel or backlit niche); the bathroom set must include a mirror and a feature wall behind the vanity, not a bare flat tile wall.
A bathtub is never placed without visible taps/fixtures and a styled surround (feature wall, cove light or stone apron); the bathroom set must include the tap set and a finished wall behind the tub.
A bathroom washbasin is never placed without a mirror above it; the bathroom set must include a mirror and a styled wall finish behind the vanity.
A bathroom washbasin is never placed without a mirror above it and a styled wall finish; the bathroom set must include a mirror and a feature wall behind the vanity.

A bathroom is never built with a plain bathtub and stone counter when the design calls for a walk-in shower with glass, rain head, hand shower on a rail and linear drain, a floating fluted vanity with lit cubbies and floor glow, and a shaped mirror; the bathroom set must match the project's design language.
Interior doors are never rendered as plain unadorned wooden slabs with basic round knobs; each door must carry a distinct product model with a handle set that matches the room's style.

A bathroom is never rendered with a plain large-format tiled wall, a round mirror and a stone basin on a dark frame without an illuminated mirror, a lit open niche with toiletries, a towel rail, a cove light and under-vanity light; the bathroom set must include these styled elements.

A bathroom is never rendered with a plain light-tile wall, a plain round mirror, no dark fluted WC wall or stone apron feature wall, no towel bars and no accent-colour towels; the bathroom set must include a feature wall, a shaped mirror, towel bars and styled towels.
An interior bathroom is never built without a window or a borrowed-light opening; if the plan shows no window, a high borrowed-light window or an interior glazing must be added to provide daylight.
Interior doors are never rendered fully closed in a hall view; where nothing stops them, inside doors must be shown open by default so the room beyond is visible.

A drawn cluster larger than 4.5 m on a side is a group of pieces, not a single untyped piece: the reading stage must split it into its member pieces (or mark it as a group) before typing, instead of leaving one oversized untyped blob for review.

When a plan labels a roof terrace with a door to it but the section draws the roof closed over it, the build stage must cut the roof over the terrace footprint (a roof terrace) instead of leaving the roof solid.
A door whose top reaches over the roof underside at its wall must be clipped to the roof underside (or a dormer added) so it does not show through the roof.
A door whose top is above the roof underside at its wall must be clipped to the roof underside so it does not show through the roof.
A parametric placeholder model that renders as a crude low-poly box must be swapped for a library model of the same type and footprint when one is available.
A parametric placeholder that renders as a crude or misplaced object must be swapped for a library model of the same type and footprint when one is available.
A kitchen counter run under a window or along a wall must be completed with wall cabinets or tall units above it so the wall is not left blank and unbalanced.
Living rooms must have a feature wall (panelling, wainscot or accent finish) behind the main seating and TV wall; flat untextured concrete is not acceptable.
An interior bathroom camera must frame the main group (bathtub, washbasin, toilet) so the room reads as a bathroom, not a bare corner.
Bedrooms must have a feature wall (vertical fluted or slatted wood panelling) behind the bed; flat untextured paint is not acceptable.
Living rooms must have a feature wall (vertical wood panelling or wainscot) behind the main seating; flat untextured paint is not acceptable.
Beds must be dressed with layered bedding (throw, second blanket, euro shams, decorative cushions); a single flat duvet is not acceptable.
A sofa model that looks like a crude blocky placeholder must be swapped for a library model of the same type and footprint that matches the project style.
A dining table that collides with a chair by more than the tolerance must be swapped for a model with a smaller footprint or different leg geometry that clears the chair.
A washbasin model that renders as a crude low-poly box must be swapped for a library model of the same type and footprint with a realistic curved basin.
Bathrooms must have warm layered lighting and a dark accent wall to match the reference style; flat beige with cold grey metal hardware is not acceptable.
For a hall whose only camera is refused by the pose solver, do not re-ask set_camera; flag the room for a program/layout change (add a console or mirror, or re-solve) instead.
When set_camera is refused for every pose of a room, the finding is a room-program/layout issue, not a camera issue; do not retry set_camera.

Kitchen and living surfaces should carry a small set of styling props (bowl, board, small appliance, books, vase) as part of the room's finished look; the furniture stage should place these props on counters and tables, not leave them bare.
Armchairs in a living room should share the design language (style tags) of the main sofa; the fit stage should prefer models whose style tags overlap the sofa's.
Sofas and beds should carry cushions, pillows and a throw as part of the finished look; the furniture stage should add these soft-furnishing props to seating and sleeping groups.

Windows in living and bedroom rooms should carry layered curtains (sheer + drape on a ceiling track) as part of the finished look; the furniture/decoration stage should add window treatments to full-height windows.
Bathroom cameras should frame the room's main fixture group (basin, toilet, cabinet) rather than a single corner; the camera stage should pick poses that show the functional set.
Bathroom cameras should frame the room's main fixture group (basin, toilet, shower) rather than a single corner; the camera stage should pick poses that show the functional set.
When set_camera is refused for every pose of a small bathroom (duplicate or no free point), the finding is a room-size/layout issue, not a camera issue; do not retry set_camera.

Bedroom furniture (bed, bench, wardrobe) should share a design language and palette that matches the room's wall colour and the project's modern standard; the fit stage should reject models whose style tags (e.g. 'classic', 'ornate') conflict with the room's modern palette, and the decoration stage should add feature walls, bedding and art.
Every large exterior window (glazing wider than 1.5 m) must be dressed with a full-height layered curtain treatment (sheer plus drape) in the render, so no large window is shown as bare glass.

In every living room, the wall behind the main seating (the wall the sofa or sideboard faces) must be finished as a feature wall (fluted or slatted wood panelling or wainscot), not a single flat paint colour.
Coffee tables and sideboards in living rooms must be styled with curated objects (a mirror, vase, leaning art print, books) in the render, never left bare.
Potted plants and other decor placed in a room must be visible in the render (not hidden behind walls or out of frame); bare long walls and corners must be filled with visible decor.
Every camera view must show the furniture and decor that belong to its room; a view dominated by an out-of-focus foreground element (curtain, plant) that blocks the room's contents is not acceptable.

Exterior renders must use warm, directional lighting (not flat overcast grey), show warm light from windows, and include the full exterior styling (landscaping, materials, details) set by the reference.
Large ground-floor glazing on the main facade must show warm interior light in exterior renders, so the facade does not look like a dead dark void.
Exterior renders must have appealing lighting, real landscaping (not a green void), and facade material richness matching the reference style.
Exterior renders must be styled (warm lighting, landscaping, furniture, materials) to match the reference; a raw grey-box massing study is not client-ready.
Exterior renders must have textured materials, warm directional lighting (not flat and foggy), and a designed landscape (not a featureless void).
Site/aerial views must show material richness (wood, glass, metal), landscape design (planters, paths, lighting), and warm lighting; a raw massing study with a textureless lawn is not acceptable.

A decor item that cannot rest on its host within tolerance (gap or penetration) must be dropped from the scene, not left as a failed build; the rest check already rejects it, so the scene stage should silently omit it instead of reporting it as a finding.

The reading stage must read entities on layers that are off or frozen (or invisible) when the ledger shows they hold geometry the model needs; a layer being off in the source file is not a reason to skip its entities.
guards.target: # entities on layers that are off or frozen (or invisible) were not read

guards.rule: A camera that is dropped must carry a reason (e.g. 'redundant with ext_3', 'blocked by geometry', 'outside the building envelope'); a camera dropped with no reason is a loss that must be explained.
An exterior camera that must show a given window is posed to frame that window; a window missing from a required view is a camera framing error, not a missing window.

A small drawn block (under ~0.7 m) on a level that already has its functional set built (a bathroom with its full set, a hall with its stair) is a detail or annotation, not a missing element; the ledger should not flag it as lost.
A stair block drawn on a level where a stair is already built in the model is a duplicate or annotation, not a missing element.
A block under 0.3 m is a detail (fixture, symbol, annotation), not a missing element.
A block with a non-descriptive name (e.g. 'eeere') and a size matching a common furniture piece already present in the room is a duplicate or annotation, not a missing element.
A block with a non-descriptive name and a size matching a large furniture piece already present in the room (e.g. a bed or sofa) is a duplicate or annotation, not a missing element.
A block under 0.7 m with a non-descriptive name is a detail or annotation, not a missing element.
A block under 0.8 m with a non-descriptive name is a detail or annotation, not a missing element.
A site decor block (TEFRIŞ = decoration) recorded by site decor elements (sd_*) is intentionally not built as a model element; it is a site annotation.
A small drawn block (under ~0.7 m) on a level that already has its functional set built is a detail or annotation, not a missing element.

When the source DWG has entities on off, frozen or invisible layers, the reading stage must list them in the ledger as 'not read (layer state)' and the audit must treat them as a source-data note, not a lost-element finding, unless a later check shows a specific missing element that the frozen layer would have supplied.
A drawn symbol that two independent passes both classify as not furniture is correctly kept as a non-built obstacle; the ledger warning is informational, not a loss.

A wall-layer selection warning that documents the chosen layer and its evidence is informational; columns that stand out of the wall band are structural, not furniture, and are not modelled as pieces.
A drawn element on a structural layer (A-BA) classified as a column is correctly not built as furniture; the ledger warning is informational.
A drawn element that is 60% or more inside a larger built fixture is correctly treated as a duplicate or part of that fixture and not built separately.
Two floor lamps of the same room that overlap are one lamp drawn twice; the larger one is kept and the smaller duplicate is not built.

A layer of generic 2D entities (circles, lines) that is not referenced by any room, piece, or opening is auxiliary drawing content (dimensions, annotations, or construction lines) and is correctly not modelled.
A 2D decoration/hatch layer (floor or wall finish pattern) is not a built element: the model carries the finish in the material slot, so its entities are neither built nor warned.
A drawn piece that is typed correctly but has no model assigned must be fitted with a library model of matching size and style so it is built, not left as 'model none'.
A piece present in the decor stage must survive the agent stage: the agent must not drop a placed piece that the documents show, only reposition or retype it.

A room whose label names a multi-use activity/leisure space (e.g. 'Oyun Aktivite Ve Dinlenme Odası') must be typed 'living', not 'other', so that standard living-room furniture (sofa, armchair, bench, table) is allowed and verified instead of kept unverified.

When one room outline carries two room labels (e.g. 'Salon' and 'AÇIK MUTFAK'), the reading must split the outline into the two rooms at the wall between them (or, if no wall is drawn, keep the larger-area label and record the second as an open-kitchen zone) instead of silently keeping only the largest label.

An exterior camera that frames a facade must be posed so that windows read as windows (clear sightline, not occluded by a mullion, frame or adjacent element); a window that renders as 'other_object' in an exterior view indicates the camera or the window model is wrong and must be corrected before the view is accepted.

A drawn piece whose model footprint differs from its drawn footprint must be placed so its centre matches the drawn centre within tolerance; if the model is larger, the layout must shift it back to the drawn centre rather than leaving it offset.

A drawn piece whose drawn size differs from the fitted model by more than 0.05 m must be resized to its drawn size (or fitted with a model of that size) before the layout solver is allowed to move it; a move that only hides a size mismatch is refused.

A drawn bed whose drawn width exceeds 1.80 m is a king-size bed and must be fitted with a king-size model (or resized to the drawn width); a standard double model is not a valid fit for a drawn king footprint.

A chair drawn at a dining table must keep its drawn position and orientation relative to the table; the layout solver may not move or rotate a drawn chair to satisfy a generic 'face the table' rule when the drawing already shows the intended pose.

A zone label that names a kitchen (e.g. 'AÇIK MUTFAK', 'OPEN KITCHEN') inside a living room outline must be read as a kitchen zone: the reading stage classifies the labelled area as a kitchen sub-zone so the open kitchen is kept and its fixtures are placed, rather than leaving it as an unclassified label.
A door whose opening no library model fits is built parametric in the house's door family; that is the correct fallback and is not a finding.
When every candidate library model for a piece is refused by the fit rules or removed by audit, the piece is built parametric and the finding is closed as a library gap rather than retried.
When a piece is built from the parametric family, the fit stage must first try the library models that match its size and room style; the parametric mesh is the fallback, not the default.
The kitchen module builder must align the joints of wall cabinets with the joints of the base units below them, so that the vertical seams match.
The lighting rule must hang the calculated number of ceiling lights (6) in a living room of 50.9 m², not fewer.
The decor stage must place a TV in a bedroom if there is a suitable wall space, or explicitly mark the room as TV-free if the design intent is to omit it.
The layout stage must include storage (e.g., a tall cabinet or shelf) in a bathroom set, not just the fixtures.
The decor stage must apply a fluted panel or similar feature to the accent wall in a bedroom to meet the professional bar (UL106).

A room typed 'living' always receives the full professional dressing (accent-wall feature panel and layered sheer+opaque curtains) even when its label names a different use; the type, not the label, drives the finish set.

Every bed_double in a modern bedroom is dressed with the full bedding set including a woven, fringed throw across its foot; the throw is generated by the bedding plan, never left to a separate placement step.

The bedding dressing step must produce a smooth, taut duvet surface on every bed_double (no lumps or wrinkles exceeding 6 mm over 0.30 m) before any throw or cushion is placed; a lumpy duvet is a dressing failure, not a model choice.

In any room typed 'living', the tv_unit is always a floating or wall-mounted console (per P16/R45); a floor-standing TV unit is not allowed in a living room and the decor stage must select a wall-hung model.
Every sofa group in a room typed 'living' must be placed on a rug (per UL106 and P16 R48); the decor stage's living-dining details always include a rug under the seating group.

Kitchen countertops must use a textured stone material (marble_slab, travertine, or similar) rather than a flat, untextured grey; the material assignment stage must select a rich stone look for kitchen counters.
All chairs in a dining group must use the same model or a matching set; the decor stage must assign a single chair model to every chair around a dining table to maintain set coherence.

Door materials must be consistent with the room's material palette; a door's finish must not clash with the dominant floor and wall materials of the room it serves. The material assignment stage must check door finishes against the room's palette.
Terraces and balconies longer than 3 m must include decking, planters, or accent elements to break up the paving; the decor stage must add these as part of the terrace dressing.

Terrace and balcony views must have a textured landscape background (trees, hedge, or garden) rather than a flat, untextured green plane; the site dressing stage must add a textured background to all outdoor views.
All balconies and upper terraces must include planters or greenery to soften the hard stone and glass; the decor stage must add planter boxes with plants to every balcony.
A desk in a bedroom or study that has a seat facing it must carry a work set (laptop or computer) on its top, oriented to the seat, so the workstation reads as used.
A drawn outline larger than 4.5 m on a side that encloses other pieces is a zone or rug mark, not a furniture piece; the build stage must not build it as a piece.
When both recognition passes classify a drawn symbol as not_furniture, the build stage correctly keeps it as an obstacle and does not build it as a piece.
A drawn outline that encloses a table and chairs and is identified as a rug mark is not a furniture piece; the decor stage handles rug placement.
When two floor lamps of the same room overlap by more than 15%, they are one lamp drawn twice; the larger footprint is kept and the smaller duplicate is not built.
A small ottoman drawn more than 50% inside an armchair or sofa is its seat cushion or part of that piece, not a separate furniture item; it is not built independently.
A piece removed by an explicit AI.remove_piece decision is not built; the removal is intentional and the finding is a record of that decision.
A large outline (over 3 m on a side) that encloses other pieces is a rug or zone mark, not a furniture piece; the decor stage handles rug placement.
The upper end of a stair that arrives at the top level of the building is not built as a separate piece; the stair is already represented by its lower-level instance.
A ceiling light must be hung from the ceiling with a cord or rod and a canopy; a gap greater than 0.02 m between its top and the ceiling is a defect.
A cushion placed on a bed must rest on its surface; penetration deeper than 0.03 m is a defect.
When one room outline holds the labels of several rooms, the reading must split it into separate rooms at the internal walls; a label with no room of its own is a lost room.

A ledger A1 'no room uses this label' is a false alarm when a room of the same level and function already exists at the label's anchor with a larger outline; report it as a size mismatch, not a lost room.

A ledger A1 'no room uses this label' is a false alarm when a room of the same level and function already exists at the label's anchor within 1 m² of the label's area; report it as a size mismatch, not a lost room.
A balcony or terrace room must have its terrace_lounge group placed; an empty outdoor space is a failed fit, not a taste issue.

Any floor opening (stairwell, void, or mezzanine edge) that drops to a lower level must have a guard (railing or glass pane) at least 1.10 m high built along its open edge; the build stage must detect floor openings and add guards automatically.

Decor elements must be clipped or repositioned so their top does not exceed the roof line (ridge height minus a 0.1 m clearance); the build stage must check decor heights against the roof and refuse or adjust any element that pokes through.
An interior camera must show at least one main fixture or piece of the room; a black or empty frame is a failed camera and must be repositioned to show the room's content.
Scene check failures (S5) indicate geometry or placement errors; the build stage must be re-run to resolve them.
Sofa and soft-seat models must have their parts joined within 1 cm; the build stage must re-run soft_seats.join_parts if parts are separated by more than 1 cm.
Scene check failures (S1) indicate geometry errors; the build stage must be re-run to resolve them.
Scene check failures (S2) indicate geometry errors; the build stage must be re-run to resolve them.
A scene check that fails on a level is a build-stage defect: re-run the build for that level so the geometry is regenerated and re-checked.

When every rotation of a drawn piece is refused because it cannot face its group without breaking another rule, the furniture agent's next round must re-solve the whole seating group (sofa, coffee table, armchairs) as one unit rather than rotating a single piece.
A tv_unit whose back is off a wall and whose rotation is refused must be re-placed by the furniture agent against the wall it belongs to, as part of the seating group it serves.
A piece that reaches through the room outline by 0.020 m (2 cm) is within the 0.03 m tolerance and is not a real defect.
When a drawn coffee table overlaps an armchair and every move is refused (drawn lock, max tries), the furniture agent must re-solve the seating group so the table and chairs are spaced correctly.
A piece whose front use zone is not reached by a 0.60 m walkway from the door must be re-placed by the furniture agent so the walkway is clear.
A sofa whose front use zone is not reached by a 0.60 m walkway from the door must be re-placed by the furniture agent so the walkway is clear.
When every rotation of a drawn piece is refused because it cannot face its group without breaking another rule, the furniture agent's next round must re-solve the whole seating group as one unit.
When a drawn coffee table overlaps an armchair and every move is refused (max tries), the furniture agent must re-solve the seating group so the table and chairs are spaced correctly.
A stove whose back is not on a wall must be re-placed by the furniture agent against the kitchen counter run it belongs to.
A kitchen run is placed so the working aisle in front of the counter is at least 0.90 m; if the drawn run leaves less, the run is re-solved on the same wall with the aisle met.
A stove is part of the kitchen run and its back sits on the wall; a run re-solve snaps the stove to the wall.
A sofa is placed with its long side as the seat (back on a wall); a seating group re-solve orients the sofa correctly.
A sofa's back sits on a wall; a seating group re-solve snaps it to the nearest free wall span.
An armchair in a seating group faces the group's centre; a seating group re-solve orients it.
An armchair's front use zone is kept clear; a seating group re-solve places the chairs so their fronts are not blocked.
A dining chair has at least 0.81 m behind it to the wall or piece; a dining group re-solve places the chairs with that clearance.
A double bed has at least 0.60 m free on each side; a sleeping_double group re-solve places the bed with that clearance.
A wardrobe has at least 0.80 m free in front for the doors to open; a storage group re-solve places it with that clearance.
A drawn shower whose footprint is not a real product size is a misread bay: fix it to the nearest real shower size that fits the bay, not a parametric stretch.
When a bed's side clearance is under 0.60 m, swap to a narrower bed model that fits the room instead of moving the bed off its drawn wall.

A wardrobe whose front clearance is under 0.80 m and whose wall has no free span within 1.2 m of its drawn place is a room-program conflict: the room is too narrow for a full-depth wardrobe on that wall, so the wardrobe must be swapped to a shallower model or the room re-laid out, not nudged.
When a wardrobe's front clearance is under 0.80 m, swap to a shallower wardrobe model that fits the room instead of moving the wardrobe off its drawn wall.

An armchair that stands behind the back of its seating group and cannot be rotated to face the group without facing a wall is a group-layout conflict: the room's seating group must be re-solved as a unit, not the single chair rotated.
A sofa whose front free zone is blocked by another sofa (a double-sofa layout) is a group-layout conflict: the two sofas must be re-solved as one seating group, not one sofa moved.
A coffee table that is not in front of the sofa and cannot be moved more than 0.3 m (drawn lock) is a group-layout conflict: the seating group must be re-solved as a unit, not the table nudged.

An armchair that is off-angle and too far from the coffee table and cannot be moved more than 0.3 m (drawn lock) is a group-layout conflict: the seating group must be re-solved as a unit, not the chair nudged.

A tv_unit whose back is 1.01 m off a wall and whose walls have no free span (doors, windows) is a room-program conflict: the room's walls are too interrupted for a wall-mounted tv_unit at its drawn place, so the tv_unit must be re-solved with the seating group or the room re-laid out.

An armchair that stands behind the back of the tv_unit and cannot be rotated to face the group without facing a wall is a group-layout conflict: the seating group must be re-solved as a unit, not the single chair rotated.
A coffee table that is not between the sofa and its TV is a group-layout conflict: the seating group must be re-solved as a unit, not the table nudged.

Site areas that the documents label and outline (pools, sunning terraces, parking) must be built as site geometry (pool basin with coping/deck, terrace platform, parking slab) at their drawn outline; a labelled site area with no outline in the model is a loss, not an optional omission.

When two levels are read at the same elevation and hold near-identical duplicate rooms, the reading has split one floor into two; merge them into a single level instead of building a duplicated floor.
The agent stage must not drop a drawn piece of a room's seating set; a dropped piece is a loss, not a detail.
A planned kitchen piece (stove) must be built; a planned piece with no scene object is a build loss.
A planned kitchen piece (sink) must be built; a planned piece with no scene object is a build loss.
A drawn piece that is a duplicate of a larger same-type piece (one lamp drawn twice) is a detail, not a loss; the larger piece stays.
A drawn piece that is a seat cushion of a larger same-type piece (one armchair drawn with its cushion) is a detail, not a loss; the larger piece stays.
A stair core room whose only camera point is inside the stair is shown from the adjacent hall, not from inside the stair; the hall's camera must include the stair.
A drawn stove block on a level must be built; a drawn block with no model element is a loss.
A drawn toilet block on a level must be built; a drawn block with no model element is a loss.

A drawn block that duplicates a fixture the room already builds (same type, same room, within 0.5 m of the built one) is a drawing duplicate, not a lost element: the ledger must not flag it as unused.
A drawn piece whose type is correct but whose model is 'none' (no library model assigned) must be fitted to a library model of its type in the next furniture round, not left unbuilt.
An interior room camera must be posed to show every door of that room; if a door is not in the frame, the camera is re-aimed to include it.

A drawn piece in a kitchen that is too small to be a fixture (under 0.40 m on its long side) and sits beside the counter is a small appliance or stool: the reading must type it (e.g. bar_stool or a small appliance) or record why it is not furniture, never leave it 'unknown' with no warning.

A stair layer (A-MERDIVEN) that the model already represents with a built stair element is a drawing source, not a lost element: the ledger must mark it as consumed by the stair and not flag it as unused.

A stair elevation/section layer (A-merdiven görünüş) that the model already represents with a built stair element is a drawing source, not a lost element: the ledger must mark it as consumed by the stair and not flag it as unused.

Decorative tile layers (Deko_Vitrifiye, Piu_Vitrifiye) must be read as finish data: either mapped to a material slot (wet_walls, splashback, floor) or explicitly logged as decorative texture, never silently dropped without a warning.

The agent stage must not drop a drawn bathroom fixture (tall_cabinet) when the room's program requires it; if placement fails, the piece must be kept in a valid fallback position or the failure must be escalated, not silently removed.
When a host piece is not built, its dependent decor elements must not be silently dropped; the build stage must either build the host or explicitly log each dependent as lost with a reason.
Furniture symbols on the A-TEFRIS layer must be read and built as furniture, not treated as unbuildable; the build stage must not skip drawn furniture symbols without a valid reason.

Site areas labeled in the plan (parking, terrace, pool) must be built as site geometry (paving, pool outline, terrace slab) or explicitly logged as not built with a reason; the build stage must not treat them as exterior labels and skip them.
A stove drawn 0.06 m off its wall with its back parallel is a drawing gap; the reading stage must snap it to the wall.

A toilet with 0.33 m clearance to a side wall (needs 0.38 m) in a 5.0 m2 bathroom is a room-size constraint, not a model problem; the reading stage must flag the room as too small for the drawn fixture layout, and the build stage must not swap models to fix a clearance that is a function of room geometry.

A bathtub with 0.28 m clearance in front (needs 0.53 m) in a 5.0 m2 bathroom is a room-size constraint; the reading stage must flag the room as too small for the drawn fixture layout. The bathtub is drawn fixed equipment and cannot be retyped.

A toilet with 0.33 m clearance to a side wall (needs 0.38 m) in a 5.0 m2 bathroom is a room-size constraint, not a model problem; the reading stage must flag the room as too small for the drawn fixture layout.
A bathtub with 0.28 m clearance in front (needs 0.53 m) in a 5.0 m2 bathroom is a room-size constraint; the reading stage must flag the room as too small for the drawn fixture layout.
A drawn bathtub longer than the free wall span in front of it is a misread size: the fixture is resized to the real product that fits the bay, leaving the required 0.53 m clearance in front.
A drawn shower tray longer than the free wall span in front of it is a misread size: the fixture is resized to the real product that fits the bay, leaving the required 0.53 m clearance in front.
A drawn toilet wider than the free side span in its bay is a misread size: the fixture is resized to the real product that fits the bay, leaving the required 0.38 m centre-to-side clearance.
A bedroom render must show the bed as the anchor; the interior camera is re-posed to frame the bed.
A kitchen run the room already has is completed with what it misses; the fridge is a required member of the kitchen run.
A bathroom render must show its primary fixtures; the interior camera is re-posed to frame the washbasin, toilet and bathtub.
A bathroom camera must frame the room's primary fixtures (toilet, basin, tub/shower); a view that omits them is not client-ready.

A bathroom's program set must be completed to the full set drawn in the documents (tall_cabinet included) even when the room already holds a partial bathroom_set; the set-completion pass must not stop at the members it already has.

A hall's storage program is set by its function: an entrance hall takes a shoe_cabinet, but a circulation hall on an upper floor (no entrance, no shoe-off) takes no shoe_cabinet and no wardrobe; the fit stage must not place entrance storage in a non-entrance hall.
Site areas labelled in the documents (pool, sunning terrace, parking) must be built as outlines/geometry on the site; a labelled site area with no outline and no reason is a loss, not a skip.

A living room's seating group must be completed with its supporting pieces (media wall behind the tv_unit, a rug under the seating, and lighting) so the room does not read as a bare box; the fit stage must place these with the group, not leave the tv_unit floating on a bare wall.

A stair flight must be built with a continuous handrail over its full open run (with newels at turns and ends); a flight with no handrail over more than 0.72 m of its run is incomplete and must be built with its guard, not left bare.

A wall-hung item (mirror, art, unit) must not be placed over a tall piece of furniture standing in front of its wall; the wall-item pass must raise it over the furniture, move it along the wall to a free stretch, or leave it out.
A wall-hung item (mirror, art, unit) must not be placed over a window or other opening in its wall; the wall-item pass must move it to a free wall stretch or leave it out.

A hung wall item (desk unit, shelf, mirror) must never be placed over a window or door opening on its wall: the decor pass must check the opening extents on the wall and, if the item's span overlaps an opening, move it to a free wall span or leave it out.

A living room with more than 4 m of outer wall and no window or door on that wall is a blank facade: the reading must flag it and the architect must add a window or door, or the building stage must not leave a blank facade on a habitable room.
Every project must have a frontal exterior view of the entrance facade (+y direction) so the main entrance is visible in the render set.
When the terrain slopes steeper than 1:3, a retaining edge (wall, terrace, or stepped foundation) must be built to support the building and prevent erosion.
A glass balustrade on a roof terrace must be at least 1.10 m high to provide a safe guard against falling, per building codes.
A retaining wall supporting a raised garden bed must have a material that matches the building's facade (e.g., stone cladding for a stone facade), not bare concrete.
A bathroom set must include a mirror above the washbasin and a towel rail; the bathroom_set group must be defined to include these members.
A bathroom set must include a mirror above the washbasin; the bathroom_set group must be defined to include a mirror as a member.
A bathtub in a bathroom must have visible taps and mixer fixtures; the bathroom_set group must include a tap/mixer as a member, or the bathtub model must include fixtures.
The outdoor setting must have textured ground (grass, paving, etc.) and a designed horizon, not a flat untextured plane with floating sprites.
A side table on a terrace should be a designed or textured piece that matches the terrace's style, not a plain generic model.
A balcony or terrace program must be furnished as a complete outdoor lounge set (seating, table, and greenery) so the space reads as designed, not as a few isolated plants.
Every interior camera of a room must be posed to show the room's door so the entry is visible in at least one view.

An exterior camera that must show the entrance facade must be placed in the free stretch of the view line in front of the door at eye height (1.5-1.7 m); if the plot has another building on the line, the camera is placed in the nearest free gap, never inside a building.
A kitchen counter's top must sit at its working height (about 0.90-0.97 m); a model whose top is higher is a wrong model and must be refitted or swapped.
A site or aerial view keeps its role and is not re-posed to show an interior window; a window that must be seen is shown by an interior or facade view, not by the aerial site view.
A bathroom camera must frame the full fixture set (bathtub, basin, toilet) with their surroundings so the room reads as designed, not a single isolated object.
A drawn piece's orientation must match the drawing within tolerance; a 90-degree turn is a reading error corrected by rotating the piece to its drawn front.
A terrace camera must frame the furniture completely so the pieces read as finished, styled elements, not cut off at the frame edge.
Outdoor furniture on a terrace must be an outdoor-rated model (weather-resistant, appropriately scaled); an indoor glass-top table is a wrong model for the space.
Outdoor furniture on a terrace must be a curated, outdoor-rated set that matches the project's style; a generic indoor set is a wrong model for the space.

A bathroom's wet fixture must match the project's specified type (e.g. a walk-in shower with glass, rain head, and linear drain); a bathtub in place of the specified shower is a wrong type and must be retyped.
An interior camera that shows a door must frame the door open or with the room beyond visible and lit, so the view shows a space, not a closed door and a bare wall.
An interior camera that frames an interior door must show the leaf open on its swing side so the room beyond is visible, not a closed slab.
Interior doors must be rendered as a chosen product (panelled or styled leaf with a matching handle set), not a plain slab with a generic knob, and the style must be consistent per room family.

A bathroom must be furnished to a detail standard (illuminated mirror, lit open niche with toiletries, towel rail, cove or under-vanity light) rather than a plain tiled wall with a round mirror and stone basin.
Bathrooms need a feature wall behind the vanity/WC (fluted or stone apron), a shaped/framed mirror, towel bars at door and shower, and repeated accent-colour towels, not a plain light-tile wall.
A hall render that looks through an interior door must show the door open and the room beyond lit and furnished, not a closed door.
A drawn piece over 4.5 m on a side in a living room is a built-in or long low unit (e.g. a media wall or sideboard run) and must be typed as a group of standard pieces, not left untyped.
A drawn piece over 4.5 m on a side in a living room is a built-in or long low unit and must be typed as a group of standard pieces, not left untyped.
A drawn piece over 4.5 m on a side is a built-in or multi-piece run and must be typed as a group of standard pieces, not left untyped.
A door under a sloped ceiling must have at least 1.60 m headroom; where the roof slope leaves less, a dormer or raised roof is required at that wall.

A bathroom drawn with a tub may be upgraded to a walk-in shower with glass, rain head, hand shower on a rail and linear drain per the style, but a drawn fixed tub keeps its type unless the architect re-specifies it.
An interior camera that frames an interior door must show the leaf open so the room beyond is lit and furnished, not a closed door and bare wall.
A bathroom set must include its tall_cabinet; when the mirror room lacks it, the set is incomplete and the missing member must be placed.
A bathroom set must include its tall_cabinet; when the room lacks it, the set is incomplete and the missing member must be placed.
A sofa with no front set must be oriented so its front faces the open floor towards its partner, not left unoriented.

A balcony or terrace of 15 m2 or more must be furnished with a terrace_lounge group (at least two seats and a table) in addition to any single chair; a single armchair is not an acceptable program for a terrace of that size.

When a door's head is above the roof underside at its wall, the build stage must clip the door to the roof underside (reduce its height) so it does not show through the roof; the door's drawn width and position are kept.

The sheets stage must resolve every question it writes to sheets/requests.json before it may end; a run that leaves questions pending must be re-run until the ledger is empty, not accepted as 'pending'.

When a long piece (sofa, bench, console) is drawn with its long side against a wall, the front is the side facing the open floor (the long side), never the short end; an AI front on the short side is a reading error and must be corrected to the long side before the piece is built.

A bench or console drawn with its back on a wall has its front facing away from that wall (the long side into the room); the front is never the short end, and a piece already facing the correct long side must not be rotated.
A built decor item that fails a scene check (S5) must be re-fitted or re-placed before the level is accepted; the scene stage must not pass a level that still holds a failing decor item.
The big loop must keep cycling while the house score can still rise; a single no-gain cycle is not a stop condition when the score is far from the target.
A stair core room whose stair fills the room has no interior camera point; its view must be taken from the adjoining hall (the room that shows the stair), not from inside the stair core.

A fitting that chooses a parametric mesh for a piece that has a real library model of the same type and size is a wrong-model choice; the real model must be used, and a parametric mesh is only a fallback when no real model fits.
A sofa drawn without a front must have its front set to the side facing the most open floor towards its seating partner, not left unoriented.

A toilet under a sloped ceiling must be fitted to the headroom at its own position (the ceiling height above the piece), not to the room's nominal floor-to-floor height; when no library model fits that headroom, the parametric family is the correct build and the 'built below the library level' flag is a false alarm.

A room whose label names a multi-use function (play, activity, relaxation) is typed 'living' and its furniture is judged against the living-room program; a bench is a valid piece of a living room, so the 'bench is not a piece of a living room' refusal is a false alarm and the room type 'other' is the misread.

A dining chair's clearance to the wall or piece behind it is measured from the chair's backrest, not its seat edge; when the drawn chair is 0.78 m from the table edge to the wall and the chair depth is 0.55 m, the backrest-to-wall clearance is 0.23 m, which is below the 0.45 m minimum, so the finding is real and the chair must be moved or the table shifted.

A tv_unit's back must be on a wall; when the drawn position is 1.01 m off the nearest wall and no free wall span exists (doors, windows block every span), the tv_unit is a misread of a wall-mounted tv or a console that belongs on a different wall, and the general rule is that a tv_unit drawn in the middle of a room with no wall behind it is a misread and must be retyped or moved to the nearest wall span.

A 5.6 m blank outer wall in a 40.5 m2 living room is a facade defect, not a furniture problem; the general rule is that a blank outer wall longer than 3 m in a habitable room must have a window or door added by the architect, and the furniture agent cannot fix it.

A nightstand in front of a window is acceptable when the window sill is at or above the nightstand's top (0.60 m); when the sill is at 0.20 m, the nightstand blocks the window and must be moved to the other side of the bed or the window sill raised; the general rule is that a nightstand in front of a window with a sill below 0.60 m is a conflict that must be resolved by moving the nightstand or raising the sill.

A coffee table overlapping an armchair by 0.12 m2 is a layout conflict; the general rule is that a coffee table must be at least 0.40 m from the front of every seat in the seating group, and when the drawn layout cannot satisfy this, the seating group must be re-solved as a unit, not the coffee table moved alone.

A sofa with no front (front_inferred) in a room with a clear open floor must have its front set to face the most open floor; the general rule is that a sofa drawn without a front in a room with a clear open floor must have its front set to face that floor, and the agent must use set_front, not move_piece or resize_piece.

A sofa's back must be on a wall; when the drawn position is 0.59 m off the nearest wall and no free wall span exists within 1.2 m of the drawn position, the sofa is a misread of a freestanding sofa or a sofa that belongs on a different wall, and the general rule is that a sofa drawn in the middle of a room with no wall behind it is a misread and must be moved to the nearest wall span or retyped.

A sofa drawn in a living room is a drawn anchor: the seating group is re-solved around it, and the agent may not move it to chase a walkway finding on a neighbour; a walkway that is blocked by the drawn sofa is a layout conflict to report, not a reason to relocate the anchor.

A drawn coffee table is locked to its drawn position (0.3 m, 1.2 m to a wall); when the drawn position does not sit in front of the sofa, the finding is a drawing/layout conflict to report, not a move the agent may make.

A washbasin that is part of a bath_set module is pinned to the module's counter: the agent may not swap its model to a freestanding one; a style finding on a module member is a style conflict to report, not a swap.

A toilet whose lowest point is 0.20 m above its floor is a parametric height error: the fix is to set its floor/height, not to swap its model; a swap that changes the height is refused by the fit rules.
A drawn bed is a drawn anchor: the agent may not move it to open a 0.60 m side walkway; a side gap that is too small is a layout conflict to report, not a move of the anchor.
A drawn coffee table that overlaps a drawn armchair by 0.12 m2 is a drawing conflict: the drawn_lock (0.3 m) forbids the move that would clear it, so the conflict is reported, not fixed by a move.

A drawn armchair that stands behind the back of the drawn sofa is a drawing conflict: rotating it to face the group is refused when it faces a wall or leaves the room, so the conflict is reported, not fixed by a rotation.

A drawn nightstand that stands in front of a window is a drawing conflict: the move that clears the window is refused (overlap with the bed, inside_room), so the conflict is reported, not fixed by a move.

A drawn wardrobe whose front clearance is 0.17 m (needs 0.80 m) is a drawing conflict: the move that opens the clearance is refused (no free wall span, still short), so the conflict is reported, not fixed by a move.

A washbasin that is part of a bath_set module and whose lowest point is 0.384 m above its floor is a module height error: the agent may not swap its model; the height must be corrected, which no tool in this run does.

A drawn piece that reaches up to 0.020 m (0.05 m2) through the room outline is within the drawing tolerance: the architect's rule F5 already says these are fine, so the critic's F9 finding on them is a false alarm and the rule needs no change.

A front use zone that is not reached by a 0.60 m walkway from a door is a layout conflict the architect must decide on: the rule C1 must state whether such a zone is acceptable (e.g. when the piece is drawn and the walkway is blocked by another drawn piece) or must be fixed.

A toilet whose centre is 0.33 m from the side wall (needs 0.38 m) is a layout conflict the architect must decide on: the rule S4 must state whether such a clearance is acceptable (e.g. when the toilet is drawn) or must be fixed.

A sofa whose free zone in front is blocked by another piece is a layout conflict the architect must decide on: the rule F4 must state whether such a blockage is acceptable (e.g. when both pieces are drawn) or must be fixed.

Rule E1 (facade openings) must require that every outer wall span of a habitable room longer than 3.0 m carries at least one window or door; a blank facade span is a defect to be resolved by adding an opening, not by re-laying out the furniture.
An interior camera of a wet room must frame the room's main fixture group (basin, bath/shower, toilet) from a free point with headroom, never a tight crop of a single corner.

A drawn fixed piece whose current library model clashes with the room's palette (cold metal hardware on a warm scheme) must be swapped for a model in the same size class whose finish matches the room's style.
A corridor camera must frame the hall's main group (storage and the doors it serves) so the passage reads as a designed hall, not an empty wall.
A shoe cabinet model that reads as a bare parametric grid of open cubbies must be swapped for a finished, closed-front model in the same size class.
A kitchen render must carry styled worktop props (fruit, board, small appliance) so the counter reads as lived-in, not bare.
A kitchen counter's worktop must carry styling props (kettle, fruit, board) to read as a complete, lived-in kitchen.
A lounge chair whose wood tone and design language clash with the room's main seating set must be swapped for a model in the same size class that matches the set's palette.
A sectional that renders as a bare shell with no cushions or throws must be swapped for a model that includes styled cushions and shams in the same size class.
Coffee and side tables in a living room must carry styled objects (books, vase, small items) to create a warm, curated feel.
Full-height windows in a living room must carry layered curtains (sheer and drape on a ceiling track) so the room does not read as exposed and unfinished.
A dining chair whose material or tone clashes with the rest of the dining set must be swapped for a model in the same size class that matches the set's palette.
An interior camera of a wet room must frame the room's main fixture group from a free point with headroom, never a tight crop of a single corner.
An interior camera of a wet room must frame the room's main fixtures (shower, toilet) from a free point, not a corner pressed to the vanity and door.
A corridor runner must be a neutral, properly proportioned rug that layers the floor, not a clashing accent that reads as a mistake.
A bedroom's nightstand and bed-side area must carry styled objects (console, mirror, vase, books) so the space reads as finished, not bare.
A desk in a bedroom work corner must be furnished as a work set (laptop or monitor, lamp, books) so it reads as a used desk, not a bare slab.
A bedroom's desk chair must match the room's calm styled set; a black mesh office chair is not allowed in a bedroom.
A bedroom's headboard wall must carry a feature finish (fluted/slatted panelling or wainscot) matching the project style; flat paint alone is not acceptable for the wall behind the bed.
An interior camera must establish the room and its main furniture; it must not be pressed against a foreground object that obscures the space.
Two sofas in one living room must not be identical clashing models; they should read as a designed set, not a showroom of one product.
Dining table and chairs must match the seating style of the room; a lighter style table against heavy bench seating is a mismatched set.
A large living-room window must carry a layered curtain treatment (sheer plus drape); bare glass is not acceptable.
A living room's seating wall must carry a feature finish (fluted/slatted panelling or wainscot) matching the project style; flat paint alone is not acceptable.
Coffee tables and sideboards in a living room must be styled with curated objects (mirror, vase, art, books), not left bare.
A seating group's armchairs and side table must be one coherent style; mixing a solid wood frame, all-rattan, and a third style is a mismatched set.
Terrace potted plants must be visible and the terrace's bare walls and corners must be dressed so the space reads as finished.
Large ground-floor glazing must show warm interior light so the facade reads as inhabited, not a dead dark void.
A bathroom camera must show the room as a whole (washbasin, cabinet, toilet, tub); a close-up of a corner is not acceptable.
A hall camera must show the space with its furniture and decor; a close-up of a corner and door frame is not acceptable.
The view outside a window must show a designed landscape (planters, seating, landscaping), not a flat low-poly green field.
A kitchen must be a complete functional set: fridge, oven, range hood, counter, sink, stove; a missing fridge or hood makes it fundamentally incomplete.
A seating group in one room must be one coherent style and colour family; a single piece of a different material or colour family is a wrong model, not a placement problem.
A full-height window wall in a living room must carry a curtain or drape layer (sheer plus drape) as part of the room's finish; a bare glass wall is an incomplete set, not a wardrobe problem.
A dining table in a furnished living/dining room must be styled with a table setting (plates, glasses, centrepiece) as part of the dining group; a bare tabletop is an incomplete set.
An interior bathroom camera must frame the room's main fixtures (bathtub or shower, toilet, washbasin) from a free point with headroom, not a corner or a single small object.
An interior hall/entrance camera must frame the hall as a space (its entry furniture and the door it leads to) from a free point, not a low-angle corner of a single door.
An office chair in a residential bedroom/desk corner must be a soft, upholstered or wood chair in the room's style, not a corporate black leather task chair.
A desk in a modern minimalist bedroom must be a clean, flat-front modern or scandinavian piece, not a traditional raised-panel Shaker desk.
A wardrobe in a scandinavian/modern bedroom must have a refined, finished surface that matches the headboard and walls, not a raw, unfinished light wood.
An interior hall camera must frame the hall as a styled space (its storage, the stair it serves) from a free point with headroom, not a bare, unstyled corridor.
A large empty wall behind a sofa in a living room must carry wall art, a feature panel or textured wallpaper as part of the room's finish; a bare wall is an incomplete set.
The site ground around a building must carry a real ground material (grass, paving, gravel) with texture, not a flat untextured plane.
An outdoor terrace floor must carry a real outdoor floor material (paving stone, decking, terracotta) with texture, not a bare untextured grey slab.
The garden/outdoor environment must carry a real ground material (grass, planting) with texture, not a flat untextured green plane.
An outdoor floor (terrace, balcony, veranda) is never left as bare untextured concrete; it is given a finished paving or decking look.
The facade is never left as a flat grey box; it is given a finished cladding or render look with a defined entrance.
A balcony or terrace is furnished with a place to sit (a lounge or seating group), not left as a bare slab.
An exterior view is framed at eye level (1.5-1.7 m) or as a high view above the ridge, never a close-up that cuts off the building.
A bedroom floor is laid in a designed pattern (herringbone or chevron), not a flat untextured slab.
A stone-clad wall is given a finished, varied stone look, not a flat repetitive placeholder texture.
An entrance door is registered in the site entrances list so it can be styled with steps, a path, and lighting.
An interior view shows the room's main group, not a tight crop of a corner.
An interior view shows the room's main group, not a partial view that misses the anchor piece.
A bedroom is furnished with a cohesive, styled set (matching bed, nightstands, wardrobe, rug, art, curtains), not a mismatched classic-modern clash.
A bedroom is furnished with a cohesive, styled set (matching bed, nightstands, wardrobe, rug, art, curtains), not a bare grey-box corner.
A decorative accessory (plant, throw, cushion) that cannot rest on the built host's top surface is dropped silently; it is not a conservation loss and needs no build.

When a bathroom set is reported complete but a member (e.g. tall_cabinet) is absent from the built room, the set-completeness check must compare against the built pieces, not the planned set, and the solver must place the missing member.
The DWG reading stage must read entities on all layers, including those that are off, frozen, or invisible, because the architect may have toggled layer visibility without removing the geometry.
guards.target: # entities on layers that are off or frozen (or invisible) were not read

guards.rule: OLE2FRAME and WIPEOUT entities are OLE/clip objects, not architectural geometry; the reading stage may skip them without a conservation loss.
The camera stage must not drop a planned exterior view without recording a reason; if a view is redundant or blocked, it must be logged with the cause.
An exterior camera that must show a specific window must be positioned so the window is in frame; if the current pose misses it, the camera is moved.
Every drawn block on a plan that is not a dimension, text, or symbol must be mapped to a model piece or explicitly recorded as not built with a reason.
Blocks smaller than 0.3 m on a side are typically symbols, fixtures, or details, not furniture; they may be skipped without a conservation loss.

A drawn INSERT whose block name is a placeholder or anonymous string (e.g. 'eeere', 'bulmak', 'A$C...') and has no label, no matching library model and no room context is a drawing artifact, not a furniture element: the reading stage records it as untyped and the ledger must not flag it as a lost element.

AutoCAD anonymous blocks (names starting with 'A$C') that are smaller than 0.10 m in any dimension are drawing artifacts (hatch boundaries, dimension fragments, annotation pieces), not furniture: the reading stage must not flag them as lost elements.

A drawn INSERT whose block name is a placeholder or anonymous string (e.g. 'eeere', 'bulmak', 'A$C...', 'DFGNHNBG') and has no label, no matching library model and no room context is a drawing artifact, not a furniture element: the reading stage records it as untyped and the ledger must not flag it as a lost element.

A drawn INSERT whose block name is a placeholder or anonymous string (e.g. 'eeere', 'bulmak', 'A$C...', 'TA161') and has no label, no matching library model and no room context is a drawing artifact, not a furniture element: the reading stage records it as untyped and the ledger must not flag it as a lost element.

A drawn INSERT that is a site decor element (e.g. 'TEFRIŞ', 'decoration', 'trim') and is already recorded as site decor (sd_*) is intentionally not built as furniture: the ledger must not flag it as a lost element.

A drawn INSERT that is a stair block (e.g. 'merdiven') and the model already has a stair in the same room or level is a duplicate/annotation block, not a missing element: the ledger must not flag it as a lost element.

AutoCAD anonymous blocks (names starting with 'A$C') that are smaller than 0.30 m in any dimension are drawing artifacts (hatch boundaries, dimension fragments, annotation pieces), not furniture: the reading stage must not flag them as lost elements.
A6 must not flag annotation-scale blocks (under ~0.10 m on a side) as lost furniture; they are dimension or text marks, not buildable elements.
A6 must not flag large landscape/site symbol blocks (over ~1.5 m, on a site or outdoor layer) as lost furniture; they are site graphics, not buildable interior elements.
A6 must not flag a small table symbol that duplicates an already-built table in the same room as a lost element; one built table satisfies the drawn set.
A6 must not flag a table symbol that duplicates an already-built table in the same room as a lost element.
A7 must not flag entities on off/frozen/invisible layers as lost; the reading correctly excludes non-active layers.
A7 must not flag OLE2FRAME and WIPEOUT entity types as lost; they are embedded objects and masks, not buildable elements.
A7 must not flag the wall-layer selection rationale or structural columns standing out of wall bands as lost furniture; columns are structure, not buildable pieces.
A7 must not flag the wall-layer selection rationale or structural columns as lost furniture.
A7 must not flag a symbol that both reading passes classify as not_furniture (kept as an obstacle) as a lost element.
A7 must not flag a symbol that both reading passes classify as not_furniture as a lost element.
A7 must not flag a piece on a structural layer (A-BA) classified as a column as lost furniture; it is structure, not a buildable piece.
A7 must not flag a piece on a structural layer (A-BA) classified as a column as lost furniture.
A drawn entity that is 60% or more inside a larger built fixture of the same room is a part of that fixture (faucet, bowl, tap) and is not a separate piece; it is suppressed, not a loss.
A drawn entity that is 60% or more inside a larger built fixture of the same room is a part of that fixture and is suppressed, not a loss.

Two floor lamps never stand inside each other; a smaller lamp footprint drawn inside a larger one of the same room is the same lamp drawn twice (base and shade) and the duplicate is suppressed, not a loss.
Two floor lamps never stand inside each other; a smaller lamp footprint drawn inside a larger one of the same room is the same lamp drawn twice and the duplicate is suppressed, not a loss.

A layer named for 2D annotation (axis bubbles, dimensions, circles) that contains only CIRCLE/LINE entities is drawing annotation, not buildable content; it is correctly left unused and needs no warning.

A layer whose name denotes a decorative floor/finish pattern (Deko, Seramik, tile) holding ARC/ELLIPSE/SPLINE/LINE is a material pattern, not buildable geometry; it is correctly left unused and needs no warning.
A layer named for a finish or decorative treatment (VITR, vitrified) holding ARC/LINE is a finish pattern, not buildable geometry; it is correctly left unused and needs no warning.
A piece present in the decor stage and named in a copied_from record must survive the agent stage; the agent must not drop a placed piece without a documented reason.
A piece present in the decor stage and named in a slot record must survive the agent stage; the agent must not drop a placed piece without a documented reason.

A room whose furniture set (sofa, tv_unit, table_dining, armchair) and area indicate a living/activity space must be typed 'living', not 'other'; a piece allowed in the room's true type must not be flagged as not-allowed because of a mis-typed room.

When one room outline carries two room labels (e.g. Salon and AÇIK MUTFAK) because the separating wall was not read, the reading must split the outline into the two labelled rooms (or flag the missing wall) rather than keep only the largest-area label and merge the rooms.

A window seen from an exterior view must render with a recognisable frame and glazing (not a bare opening or a solid panel) so that the render check does not classify it as other_object; the fit stage must verify the window's exterior appearance, not only its geometry.
A drawn piece is placed at its drawn centre; a shift beyond the 0.05 m tolerance is a layout error, not a model error.

A drawn piece is locked to its drawn centre within the 0.05 m tolerance; a model larger than the drawn footprint must be centred on the drawn centre, and neighbour overlap is resolved by moving the neighbours, not the drawn anchor.
A drawn piece is placed at its drawn centre and orientation; a shift or rotation beyond the 0.05 m tolerance is a layout error, not a model error.
An interior camera must frame every piece it lists in show fully inside the frame; a piece cut off at the frame edge is a failed pose, not a stylistic choice.

A zone label naming a kitchen (e.g. 'AÇIK MUTFAK') inside a living room outline marks an open-kitchen zone: the reading stage must classify the enclosed counter/island pieces as a kitchen zone of the room, not drop the label as unknown.
A sofa with no front set must be oriented by the code to face the most open floor towards its partner; a missing front is a fit error, not a taste choice.
A media-wall/TV-place check must not fire for a room whose plan shows no TV; the check should be skipped when the room's drawn program has no TV piece.
A parametric door built in the house's door family is an acceptable substitute when no library model fits the opening; this is not a defect.

When a piece is built below the library level (parametric mesh), the fitting stage must pick a library model of the same type and size class; a parametric fallback is a library gap to be closed by a swap.
A living or living-dining room's main seating group (sofa + coffee table) must sit on a rug sized to the group; the decor stage's salon details must place it.
A kitchen counter's top and splashback must use a richer, textured stone (marble/travertine) look, not a flat generic grey, to match the project's modern finish.
Interior door leaves must share the project's cohesive palette (painted/neutral) rather than a warm wood that clashes with cool grey tiles and terrazzo.
A terrace/balcony camera must frame the whole space (seating, planters, paving) from a higher, wider pose, not a low close-up where one armchair fills the frame.
A terrace/balcony floor must use a warm decking or textured paving look (with planters) to break up a long run, not plain grey slabs.
The background/landscape behind a terrace or exterior view must use a textured grass/ground look, not a flat untextured green plane.
Upper balconies/terrace edges must carry planters or greenery to soften the hard stone and glass; the decor stage must place them.
Windows in the reference style must use full-height curtains in two layers (a sheer behind a heavier drape); the decor stage must add both.
Door and window frames must share one consistent frame finish across the project, not mix black and bronze/gold.
An exterior door leaf must be a finished, well-detailed product (rich wood or textured finish) that reads clearly against the stone wall, not a flat dark leaf.
Side tables must carry styled, textured decor (vases/candles with real materials), never untextured placeholder cylinders.
